levelDescription.value:
By the end of Year 10 students should have had the opportunity to design and produce at least 4 designed solutions focused on one or more of the 4 technologies contexts:
• Engineering principles and systems
• Food and fibre production
• Food specialisations
• Materials and technologies specialisations.
Students should have opportunities to experience creating designed solutions for products, services and environments.
Students use design and technologies knowledge and understanding, processes and production skills and design thinking to produce designed solutions for identified needs or opportunities of relevance to individuals and local, regional or global communities. They work independently and collaboratively. Problem-solving activities acknowledge the complexities of contemporary life and make connections to related specialised occupations and further study. Increasingly, study has a global perspective, with opportunities to understand the complex interdependencies involved in the development of technologies and enterprises.
Students specifically focus on preferred futures, taking into account ethics; legal issues; social values; and economic, environmental and social sustainability factors; and use strategies such as life cycle thinking. They use critical thinking, creativity, innovation and enterprise skills with increasing confidence, independence and collaboration. Students analyse data, evaluate design ideas and technologies, respond to feedback, and evaluate design processes used to inform designed solutions for preferred futures.
Using a range of technologies including a variety of graphical representation techniques to communicate, students generate and represent original ideas and production plans in 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional representations. These techniques will be specific to the technologies context and may include scale, perspective, orthogonal and production drawings with sectional and exploded views. Students produce rendered, illustrated views for marketing and use graphic visualisation software to produce dynamic views of design ideas and designed solutions.
Students identify the steps involved in planning the production of designed solutions. They develop detailed project management plans, incorporating elements such as sequenced time, cost and action plans, to manage design tasks safely. Students apply management plans, making adjustments when necessary, to successfully complete design tasks. They identify and establish safety procedures that minimise risk and manage projects with safety and efficiency in mind, maintaining safety standards and management procedures to ensure success.

description.value: In this Year 9 Metal Technology unit, students design and manufacture an engineer’s square from aluminium or mild steel. Students develop practical skills in accurate measuring and marking out, cutting, filing, shaping, drilling, countersinking, riveting and surface finishing. They investigate existing products, develop and communicate design ideas using sketches and CAD, and make appropriate modifications within the project specifications. Throughout the unit, students learn to select and safely use workshop tools and equipment, follow risk-control procedures and evaluate the accuracy, function and quality of their finished product.

Students will individually design and manufacture a functional engineer’s square to the supplied specifications. The completed product should demonstrate accuracy, squareness, secure assembly, smooth safety edges and a high-quality surface finish. Students may personalise or adapt aspects of the design where these changes do not affect its function.

Students will also complete a project folio documenting the design and production process. The folio will include:

A design brief, success criteria and project constraints
Research and analysis of existing products
Initial sketches and proposed design improvements
A CAD model with dimensioned orthographic views
A risk assessment and material cutting list
A photographic record of the manufacturing process
Associated workshop theory and safety questions
A final evaluation and peer evaluation

Assessment will consider students’ understanding of materials, tools and production processes, as well as their ability to generate ideas, work safely, manufacture accurately, manage time and evaluate the completed solution.

conditions.value:
• Project folio: up to 7 A4 pages or equivalent digital format, including sketches, CAD documentation, and photographic records
• Manufacturing task: in-class production under supervised workshop conditions
• Safety compliance: must adhere to all St Brendan’s College Workshop Safety protocols, including mandatory PPE and tool-specific induction logs
• Timeframe: 10-week development and construction period, inclusive of planning and evaluation phases

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students explain how people consider factors that impact on design decisions and the technologies used to design and produce products, services and environments for sustainable living. They explain the contribution of innovation, enterprise skills and emerging technologies to global preferred futures. For one or more of the technologies contexts, students explain the features of technologies and their appropriateness for purpose, and create designed solutions based on an analysis of needs or opportunities. Students create, adapt and refine design ideas, processes and solutions and justify their decisions against developed design criteria that include sustainability. They communicate design ideas, processes and solutions to a range of audiences, including using digital tools. Students independently and collaboratively develop and apply production and project management plans, adjusting processes when necessary. They select and use technologies skilfully and safely to produce designed solutions.

moderation.value:
Internal moderation is conducted systematically across the Year 10 Industrial Technology faculty to ensure consistency of teacher judgement against the Australian Curriculum achievement standards. This process involves:

*   **Production Standards Moderation:** A scheduled workshop "benchmarking" session in Week 8 where teachers compare physical student work samples against the "Engineers Square" success criteria to ensure objective and consistent application of the marking guide.
*   **Final Grade Calibration:** Departmental meeting in Week 10 to review borderline student folios and final products, ensuring the alignment of summative evidence with the Year 10 achievement standards for Materials and Technologies Specialisations.

description.value: In this Year 9 Metal Technology unit, students design and manufacture a functional junior hacksaw from solid metal bar. Students develop practical workshop skills including measuring and marking out, cutting, filing, bending, drilling, thread cutting, assembly and surface finishing. They learn to select and safely use appropriate hand tools, portable power tools and workshop equipment. Students also follow a design process to investigate existing products, develop and communicate design ideas using sketches and CAD, plan production and evaluate the quality and functionality of their completed product.

Students will manufacture a functional junior hacksaw to the supplied specifications, incorporating appropriate personalisation or design improvements. The practical project will be assessed on accuracy, functionality, quality of finish, application of production procedures, time management and safe workshop practices.

Students will also complete a project folio containing:

A design brief, success criteria and identified constraints
Research and analysis of existing junior hacksaws
Initial sketches and proposed design improvements
A CAD model and dimensioned orthographic drawings
A risk assessment and material cutting list
A photographic record of the manufacturing process
An evaluation of the completed product and production processes
Peer and self-evaluation
Associated theory questions covering workshop safety, tools, equipment, filing, corrosion protection and thread cutting

conditions.value:

• Completed junior hacksaw prototype verified against functional specifications
• Supervised workshop conditions for practical manufacturing sessions
• Internal moderation: Standardisation of marking across the 9–10 Design and Technologies faculty to ensure consistent application of QCAA achievement standards.

description.value: In this unit, students design and manufacture a functional letter box from Galvabond sheet metal. Students develop practical metalworking skills through accurate marking out, cutting, folding, joining and finishing processes. Key techniques include forming safety edges, producing double-folded and grooved seams, and cutting an external thread. Students also learn to safely select and use appropriate hand tools, portable power tools and workshop equipment. Throughout the unit, students document the design and production process in a folio, including research, sketches, CAD drawings, risk assessment, material calculations, photographs and evaluation.

Students design and manufacture a Galvabond letter box based on the supplied project specifications. The finished product must be functional, accurately constructed and include appropriate sheet-metal joining and finishing techniques. Students may personalise aspects of the design while maintaining the required dimensions and construction requirements.

Students also complete a folio documenting the development and manufacture of their letter box. The folio includes:

Design brief, success criteria and constraints
Research into existing letter box designs
Initial sketches and proposed improvements
CAD model and dimensioned orthographic drawings
Risk assessment
Material cutting list and costing
Photographic production procedure
Evaluation, peer feedback and personal reflection
Associated theory questions covering workshop safety, tools, Galvabond, sheet-metal seams and thread cutting

Assessment considers students’ knowledge and understanding, development of design ideas, safe workshop practices, production skills, accuracy, time management and evaluation of the completed product.

conditions.value:
• 6–8 A4 pages or equivalent digital media portfolio (folio)
• Product: One functional Galvabond letterbox (max dimensions 300mm x 300mm x 400mm)
• Folio to include: design brief, research, CAD orthographic drawings, risk assessment, production photos, and evaluation
• Workshop practical demonstration under supervised conditions
• Time allocated: 6 weeks of in-class construction and documentation

Internal moderation is conducted systematically within the Manual Arts department to ensure consistency of teacher judgement against the Australian Curriculum achievement standards. This process involves:

description.value:
Unit description

In this Year 9 Metal Technology unit, students design and manufacture a wrought-iron pot plant stand. They develop practical metalworking skills through marking out, cutting, filing, bending, twisting, scrolling and hard riveting steel components. Students learn to select and safely use appropriate hand tools, workshop equipment and metal-forming machinery while following established risk-control procedures. Alongside construction, students produce a design folio documenting their research, design development, CAD drawings, planning, production processes and evaluation of the completed product.

Assessment description

Students are required to design and manufacture a functional and aesthetically pleasing wrought-iron pot plant stand based on the supplied specifications. The stand must demonstrate accurate construction, effective use of scrolling and twisting techniques, secure joining methods and appropriate personalisation.

Students will also complete a folio containing:

A design brief, success criteria and identified constraints
Research and analysis of existing products
Initial sketches and proposed design modifications
A final CAD model with dimensioned orthographic views
A risk assessment and control measures
A materials cutting list
A photographic record of the production process
Responses to associated metalworking theory questions
A personal and peer evaluation of the finished product

Assessment will consider the quality and functionality of the completed stand, the application of safe workshop practices, practical production skills, design development, time management and the quality of the supporting folio.

• Monitoring: Mid-unit progress review (Week 5).
• Conferencing: Final folio and product review (Week 9).
